course.title: Academic Communication and Professional Writing
course.credit_system: ScrollUniversity workload units (ECTS workload benchmark only; not ECTS credit)
course.description: Develops clear, evidence-based academic and professional communication across written, oral and digital formats.

outcomes.text: Analyze audience, purpose, genre and evidence requirements before composing.
Construct coherent arguments using claims, evidence, reasoning and appropriate structure.
Integrate and attribute source material accurately using paraphrase, summary and selective quotation.
Produce concise professional documents and presentations adapted to stakeholder needs.
Revise communication for clarity, logic, tone, accessibility and correctness.

lessons.title: Rhetorical situation and genre
lessons.teaching_material: Effective communication starts before drafting. The writer identifies who must act or understand, what outcome is required, what constraints apply, and what evidence the audience expects. Genre is a practical contract: a research report, policy memo, reflective essay and executive email organize information differently because readers use them differently. Strong writers adapt depth, terminology, tone and structure to the communication situation rather than using one style everywhere.
lessons.activity: Rewrite the same 150-word message for a lecturer, a senior manager and a general public audience; annotate the changes you made and why.

self_check.q: Why is audience analysis necessary?
self_check.a: It determines the level of detail, terminology, tone, evidence and structure most likely to achieve the communication purpose.

self_check.q: What is genre in practical writing?
self_check.a: A recurring form with conventions shaped by how a particular audience expects to use the document.

lessons.title: Claims, reasons and evidence
lessons.teaching_material: An argument is more than a strong opinion. It links a claim to reasons and then to evidence that makes those reasons credible. Good reasoning also states assumptions and addresses relevant alternatives or counterarguments. Paragraphs become persuasive when readers can see why the evidence supports the claim, not merely that a citation appears nearby. Overclaiming weakens credibility, so conclusions should remain within the scope of the evidence presented.
lessons.activity: Create an argument map with one thesis, three reasons, supporting evidence for each and one credible counterargument.

self_check.q: What is the difference between a reason and evidence?
self_check.a: A reason explains why the claim should be accepted; evidence provides factual or scholarly support for that reason.

self_check.q: Why address counterarguments?
self_check.a: It tests the argument against plausible alternatives and shows that the conclusion was not reached by ignoring contrary evidence.

lessons.title: Document architecture
lessons.teaching_material: A strong document has visible architecture. Introductions establish the problem, purpose and direction; sections group related reasoning; conclusions answer the central question rather than merely repeat earlier sentences. Headings should describe content rather than decorate it. Ordering can follow logic such as problem-solution, cause-effect, chronology or claim-evidence. The best structure minimizes the mental work required for a reader to understand the writer's reasoning.
lessons.activity: Take an unstructured set of ten notes and turn it into a hierarchical outline with section purposes and a one-sentence thesis.

self_check.q: What should a conclusion do?
self_check.a: Answer the central question, synthesize the reasoning and state appropriate implications or next steps.

self_check.q: When is chronology useful?
self_check.a: When sequence over time is necessary to explain a process, event or development.

lessons.title: Coherent paragraphs and transitions
lessons.teaching_material: Paragraph coherence comes from a controlling idea, relevant supporting material and explicit relationships between sentences. A topic sentence normally establishes the paragraph's analytical job. Evidence should be interpreted rather than dropped into the text without explanation. Transitions are most useful when they name relationships such as contrast, consequence, example, qualification or continuation. Mechanical transition words cannot repair a paragraph whose ideas do not logically belong together.
lessons.activity: Revise a five-paragraph draft so every paragraph has one clear analytical purpose and every transition describes the relationship to the previous idea.

self_check.q: What is a controlling idea?
self_check.a: The main analytical point that determines which evidence and explanation belong in the paragraph.

self_check.q: Can transition words create logic by themselves?
self_check.a: No. They can signal relationships, but the underlying ideas must actually be logically connected.

lessons.title: Integrating evidence into prose
objectives: Choose between summary, paraphrase and quotation
lessons.teaching_material: Source integration should keep the writer's reasoning in control. Summary compresses a larger source, paraphrase restates a specific idea in original wording and structure, and quotation preserves exact wording when that wording matters. Each borrowed idea requires attribution. Evidence is introduced, presented and then interpreted so the reader understands its relevance. Long strings of quotations usually indicate that sources are replacing rather than supporting the writer's analysis.
lessons.activity: Write one paragraph that uses a summary, one paraphrase and one brief quotation from supplied sources, with an explanation after each evidence item.

self_check.q: When is direct quotation most justified?
self_check.a: When the exact wording is important to the analysis, definition, legal meaning or interpretation.

self_check.q: Why explain evidence after presenting it?
self_check.a: Readers need the writer to show how the evidence supports the paragraph's claim and wider argument.

lessons.title: Synthesis across sources
objectives: Organize literature by ideas rather than authors
lessons.teaching_material: Synthesis compares sources around concepts, methods, findings or disputes. Instead of writing one paragraph per author, the writer groups sources according to what they collectively show. Accurate synthesis distinguishes consensus from partial agreement and genuine disagreement. It also avoids false balance: a weak or isolated claim should not be given equal weight to a large, methodologically strong evidence base simply because both positions exist.
lessons.activity: Build a synthesis matrix for six sources using themes as columns, then write two paragraphs that integrate at least three sources each.

self_check.q: What is false balance?
self_check.a: Presenting positions as equally credible despite major differences in evidence quality or support.

self_check.q: Why use a synthesis matrix?
self_check.a: It helps identify patterns, overlaps and disagreements across sources before drafting.

lessons.title: Emails, briefs and decision memos
lessons.teaching_material: Professional communication is shaped by decision needs. Strong emails state purpose early, separate context from action, use informative subject lines and make responsibilities clear. Briefs and memos normally foreground the issue, evidence, options, recommendation and risks. Concision means removing material that does not help the reader decide or act; it does not mean omitting necessary evidence, uncertainty or consequences.
lessons.activity: Convert a 600-word narrative into a one-page decision memo containing issue, evidence, options, recommendation, risks and requested action.

self_check.q: What should an action-oriented email make explicit?
self_check.a: What is needed, from whom, by when and why it matters.

self_check.q: What does concision not justify?
self_check.a: Removing important evidence, limitations, risks or context necessary for a sound decision.

lessons.title: Presentations and data storytelling
objectives: Use visuals to support rather than replace reasoning
lessons.teaching_material: A presentation should have one governing message and a sequence that helps the audience understand why it matters. Slides are visual support, not a transcript. Charts should answer a specific question, use appropriate scales and labels, and avoid decoration that obscures the data. Spoken explanation should state what the audience should notice, why the pattern matters and what uncertainty or limitation remains. Accessibility requires readable text, contrast, alt descriptions where needed and non-color-only cues.
lessons.activity: Create a five-slide evidence briefing from a small dataset: context, key pattern, explanation, limitation and recommendation.

self_check.q: Why should a chart answer a question?
self_check.a: A purposeful chart directs attention to a meaningful comparison or pattern instead of displaying data without an analytical reason.

self_check.q: Why avoid slides full of prose?
self_check.a: Dense text competes with spoken explanation and increases cognitive load.

lessons.title: Revision from argument to sentence
lessons.teaching_material: Revision should proceed from large decisions to small ones. First test whether the document answers the task, the argument is defensible and the structure is logical. Then inspect paragraphs for coherence and evidence. Only after those issues are stable should sentence-level editing focus on clarity, concision, grammar and formatting. Proofreading a weak structure wastes effort because later restructuring will invalidate many sentence-level edits.
lessons.activity: Perform three passes on a draft: argument/structure, paragraph/evidence, then sentence/proofreading. Record one major change from each pass.

self_check.q: What is the difference between revision and proofreading?
self_check.a: Revision changes ideas, reasoning and structure; proofreading finds surface errors after substantive decisions are settled.

self_check.q: Why edit in stages?
self_check.a: It prevents time being spent polishing sentences that may later be removed or reorganized.

lessons.title: Tone, accessibility and ethical communication
objectives: Audit communication for accessibility and fairness
lessons.teaching_material: Professional tone is respectful, precise and appropriate to context; it is not necessarily formal or impersonal. Accessible communication uses meaningful headings, direct language, descriptive links, readable formatting and alternatives for visual or audio information. Ethical communication does not manipulate evidence, hide material limitations or imitate certainty that the writer does not possess. AI-assisted editing can improve wording, but the author remains responsible for meaning, confidentiality, originality and factual accuracy.
lessons.activity: Audit a document for tone, accessibility, unsupported certainty and AI-related confidentiality risks, then produce a revised version and change log.

self_check.q: Does professional tone require complicated vocabulary?
self_check.a: No. Precision and appropriateness matter more than complexity.

self_check.q: Who is responsible for errors introduced by AI editing?
self_check.a: The submitting author remains responsible for the final document and its claims.

assessments.title: Academic Argument Essay
assessments.instructions: Write a 1,500-word evidence-based argument for an academic audience using at least six credible sources and an explicit counterargument.

assessments.title: Professional Decision Memo
assessments.instructions: Produce a two-page decision memo for a defined stakeholder with issue, evidence, options, recommendation and risk section.

assessments.title: Presentation and Revision Portfolio
assessments.instructions: Deliver a six-minute evidence briefing with accessible slides and submit the revised written brief plus an editing rationale.
